As Messianic prophecy extended over many years in which many political changes took place in harmony with these, it displayed its riches by a variety more effective than if it had been manifested all at once. As the moral condition of the Jews required in each instance, so Messiah was exhibited in a corresponding phase, thus becoming more and more the soul of the nation's life: so that He is represented as the antitypical Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.3">Is 49:3</reference>).<div eID="gen17974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto David--</hi>Hengstenberg observes that Isaiah dwells more on His prophetical and priestly office, which had already been partly set forth (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.18">De 18:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.110.4">Psa 110:4</reference>). Other prophets dwell more on His kingly office. Therefore here He is associated with "David" the king: but in <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Is 11:1</reference> with the then poor and unknown "Jesse."<div eID="gen17975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteous Branch--</hi>"the Branch of righteousness" (<reference osisRef="Jer.33.15">Jr 33:15</reference>); "The Branch" simply (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.8">Zec 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.6.12">6:12</reference>); "The Branch of the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.2">Is 4:2</reference>).<div eID="gen17976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17977" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">prosper--</hi>the very term applied to Messiah's undertaking (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.13">Is 52:13</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Is 53:10</reference>). Righteousness or justice is the characteristic of Messiah elsewhere, too, in connection with our salvation or justification (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Is 53:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Da 9:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.9.9">Zec 9:9</reference>). So in the New Testament He is not merely "righteous" Himself, but "righteousness to us" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1Co 1:30</reference>), so that we become "the righteousness of God in Him" (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.3">Ro 10:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.19-2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:19-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.9">Php 3:9</reference>).<div eID="gen17977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17978" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">execute judgment and justice in the earth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.72.2">Psa 72:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">Is 9:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.1">32:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.32.18">18</reference>). In some passages He is said to come to judge, in others to reign. In <reference osisRef="Matt.25.34">Mt 25:34</reference>, He is called "the King." <reference osisRef="Ps.9.7">Psa 9:7</reference> unites them. Compare <reference osisRef="Dan.7.22">Da 7:22</reference>, 26, 27. <div eID="gen17978" type="x-p"/>

Judah ... Israel ... dwell safely--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.33.16">Jr 33:16</reference>, where "Jerusalem" is substituted for "Israel" here. Only Judah, and that only in part, has as yet returned. So far are the Jews from having enjoyed, as yet, the temporal blessings here foretold as the result of Messiah's reign, that their lot has been, for eighteen centuries, worse than ever before. The accomplishment must, therefore, be still future, when both Judah and Israel in their own land shall dwell safely under a Christocracy, far more privileged than even the old theocracy (<reference osisRef="Jer.32.37">Jr 32:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.28">De 33:28</reference>; Is 54:1-17; 60:1-22; 65:17-25; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.11">Zec 14:11</reference>).<div eID="gen17979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall be called, the Lord--</hi>that is, shall be (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>) "Jehovah," God's incommunicable name. Though when applied to created things, it expresses only some peculiar connection they have with Jehovah (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.14">Ge 22:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.17.15">Ex 17:15</reference>), yet when applied to Messiah it must express His Godhead manifested in justifying power towards us (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>).<div eID="gen17980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17981" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our--</hi>marks His manhood, which is also implied in His being a Branch raised unto David, whence His human title, "Son of David" (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.22.42-Matt.22.45">Mt 22:42-45</reference>).<div eID="gen17981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17982" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Righteousness--</hi>marks His Godhead, for God alone can justify the ungodly (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.4.5">Ro 4:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.17">Is 45:17</reference>, 24, 25). <div eID="gen17982" type="x-p"/>

Repeated from <reference osisRef="Jer.16.14">Jr 16:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.16.15">15</reference>. The prophet said the same things often, in order that his sayings might make the more impression. The same promise as in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.3">Jr 23:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.4">4</reference>. The wide dispersion of the Jews at the Babylonish captivity prefigures their present wider dispersion (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.11">Is 11:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.6">Joe 3:6</reference>). Their second deliverance is to exceed far the former one from Egypt. But the deliverance from Babylon was inferior to that from Egypt in respect to the miracles performed and the numbers delivered. The final deliverance under Messiah must, therefore, be meant, of which that from Babylon was the earnest. <div eID="gen17983" type="x-p"/>
